implementation_notes: Scala on the JVM delegates the policy family to the JDK: java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock, ReadWriteLock and StampedLock are the concrete strategies, and AnyRef#synchronized (with wait/notify) is the intrinsic monitor strategy available on every object - documented as executing the body with an exclusive lock on this. A component therefore holds an injected Lock and closes critical sections in try/finally, exactly as in Java, and the language adds nothing that removes the class. Scala's own concurrency culture points elsewhere, though: immutability plus Future/ExecutionContext or actor libraries (Pekko) avoid shared mutable state instead of synchronizing it, and that is usually the better answer. Reserve the strategized lock form for components that must stay lock-based - blocking APIs, Java interop, low-level data structures - and cannot be replaced by isolation or message passing.
pitfalls: synchronized is a single fixed strategy that blocks a carrier thread on virtual-thread runtimes and cannot be swapped later - exactly what a reusable component should not bake in.
Blocking inside a Future starves the ExecutionContext-managed pool; wrap genuinely blocking sections in blocking { } or keep the component on a dedicated dispatcher.
Scala's immutable defaults make a missing lock easy to overlook: a val that references a mutable structure (a mutable.Map behind a val field) is outside the strategy's protection.
